name: Phobos 1
significance: Phobos 1 was launched as the first of a pair of ambitious Soviet spacecraft designed to orbit Mars and land a hopper directly on its inner moon Phobos, aiming to determine the moon's composition and origin -- a question still debated today -- using an armory of remote-sensing and laser mass-spectrometry instruments. The mission ended just two months into its planned 200-day cruise: a single-character error in an uploaded ground command sequence inadvertently disabled the spacecraft's attitude-control thrusters, causing it to lose its solar lock and drain its batteries, with contact lost on 1988-09-02 and recovery attempts formally abandoned that November. Though it never returned science data, Phobos 1 became a cautionary tale in spaceflight operations about the fragility of command-sequence validation, influencing later ground-segment safeguards. Its sister craft Phobos 2 fared only marginally better -- reaching Mars orbit and returning the first close-up Phobos imagery before its own failure ended the mission weeks before the planned Phobos landing -- leaving the ambitious Phobos program's central goal of surface exploration unfulfilled until Japan's later Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) effort.
statusNote: Direct Earth->Mars transfer, no gravity assists; launched 5 days before sister spacecraft Phobos 2. A single erroneous ground command uploaded around 1988-08-28 accidentally disabled the attitude-control thrusters, causing the spacecraft to lose its Sun-lock and drain its batteries; contact was lost 1988-09-02, and recovery attempts were formally abandoned in November 1988. The 'arrival' date shown here is an estimate (no exact planned arrival date is published) derived from the mission's stated ~200-day planned transit.
